F1.Q1: Cut sandstone flags — dry, warm, sawn-square, set in a running bond with a recessed mortar joint. Not granite, not slate, not anything cold or wet.
F1.Q1_WHY: Every floor pixel sits at hue 28.4° ± 1.2° with saturation 0.54 ± 0.04 (sampled across the whole lit area, x180–628 / y14–400). That is one pigment. The only variation in the entire floor is value — p5 to p95 runs 0.25→0.69 brightness. A single warm-ochre hue at that saturation reads as sandstone or adobe. The slabs are rectangles in a coursed bond (visible at 1:1 across x300–560 / y80–300), joints ~3–4px and recessed dark, corners square and unbroken. Nothing on the face suggests bedding planes, cleavage, or grain direction, so it is a sedimentary block, sawn.
F1.Q2:
South, toward the corridor mouth at x378–432, y400+.

Nothing about the ground influenced that. I picked it because it is the only opening the light reaches — the walls stop and a gap continues. I checked the slabs in the corridor mouth (x378–432, y400–440) against the slabs the figure is standing on (x380–430, y160–200) and they are the same: same hue, same mark density, same joint treatment, same value once you correct for the torch falloff. The floor did not vote.
F1.Q3: It has been scuffed, evenly, everywhere, once — and nothing else. There is no history in it. No traffic, no spill, no repair, no settling, no place where something was dragged or stood or dropped. It has damage but no events.
F1.Q3_WHY:
I binned relative surface detail (local contrast normalised against the local mean, so the vignette can't fake it) into 16×16 cells across the whole floor. The map saturates at the top of the scale in nearly every cell. There is no low-detail region anywhere inside the light radius — not at the corridor mouth, not in the room centre, not against the walls. Wear that is uniform to that degree is not wear; it is a texture.

And the damage that exists is only ever one kind: shallow surface abrasion. Slab corners are square everywhere — check (445,215), (520,145), (300,255) — nothing is rounded, chipped, dished, or lipped. Joints are full and crisp along their whole length; nothing has been re-pointed, nothing has spalled at an edge, no slab sits proud of or below its neighbours. For a place in continuous heavy use with a garrison repairing it by hand, there is not one repair on this floor.
F1.Q4:
Two things, and both are problems.

**The blank slabs.** Roughly eight slabs inside the lit core carry no marks at all and are filled flat at almost exactly the mortar value: (530,214)–(595,235), (517,87)–(548,116), (372,125)–(405,141), (477,179)–(500,200), (455,217)–(491,231), (340,304)–(362,328), and the large one at (200,293)–(280,336). At 1:1 they are the highest-contrast features on the entire floor — dark rectangles that pull the eye off the figure. But they carry no information. They are not holes, not different stone, not shadow: I magnified (360,100)–(440,150) to 6× and the slab is a solid fill with no interior edge and no falloff. They read as slabs that missed their texture pass, and the eye keeps going back to them because they are the only large shapes present.

**The arcs.** Three or four long, thin, gently-curving dark lines cross the floor at a shallow angle, ignoring the slab joints — one runs roughly (250,375) up to (430,285), another (340,395) out to (620,300), and they cross in an X at about (385–400, 315–330). Once you see one you find the rest, and they start to read as a system laid over the floor rather than as damage in it. More on why in Q5.
F1.Q5:
**Repeated.** Specifically: a real, hand-built slab layout with a small library of decals stamped over it.

The layout itself is authored — I cross-correlated the high-passed floor against itself over every offset from 0 to 200px horizontally and 140px vertically, and there is no repeat peak (best non-adjacent value 0.165 at dx=12). Nobody tiled a bitmap. The bond pattern, the slab sizes, the courses: those were placed.

The faces were not. I binarised the surface detail with the joints masked out and searched for identical patches. A single 10×10 mark pattern occurs **32 times** across the floor. Twenty-plus distinct 10×10 patterns each occur 19–32 times. Going bigger, an identical **24×24** block appears at (467,51) and again at (467,173) — the same 576 pixels, twice, 122px apart. That is a stamp library, and it is a small one.

You can see the whole vocabulary by eye at 4× on (440,14)–(630,200): 45° hatch strokes, rows of short horizontal dashes, clusters of vertical ticks. Three motifs. They are on every slab, at the same density, in the same proportions. There is also a short-range rhythm underneath — elevated self-correlation at ~12px horizontally and ~9px vertically — so the marks land on a beat. That beat is what makes the surface read as woven cloth rather than stone at 1:1.

The arcs from Q4 are the same failure at level scale. I traced the one near (425,300) pixel by pixel: at y=301–302 it runs **perfectly horizontal for 28 pixels, x=425 through 452**, then steps away in symmetric 4px and 6px runs on both sides, at a constant 2px width the entire way. That is a rasterised parabola. A fracture has a width that varies, an origin, branches, a termination, and something on one side displaced relative to the other. This has a flat apex.
F1.Q6:
**YES.** Plenty of shipped games have floors exactly this good. The bond is convincing, the values are controlled, the lighting sits on it correctly, and it does not read as broken.

Merely competent. Not good. It is a texture that survives being looked at and gives you nothing for looking.
F1.Q7:
**The faces are effectively blank at 1:1.** What is legible is layout and value, not surface.

Legible without magnifying, from the full 750×600 view:
- the slab layout and joints (everywhere)
- the value differences between slabs — some flags lighter, some darker
- the long arcs (the one through (250,375)→(430,285) is genuinely readable)
- the blank dark slabs from Q4
- a fine woven grain over everything, the way hessian reads across a room — present, uniform, and not resolvable into anything

That last item is the whole answer. I could see *that* the faces had texture. I could not see *what* the texture was.

Only on magnification:
- that the grain is 45° hatch strokes at all
- the rows of short horizontal dashes
- the vertical tick clusters — these are the interesting ones, they read almost like scored inscription, tallies cut into the stone, exactly the mark an administered underworld would leave. At 1:1 they are completely invisible. I found them at 3× in (440,14)–(630,200) and had to go back and hunt for them elsewhere. That counts as hunting.
F1.Q7_WHY: Checked at 1:1 — the whole floor as rendered, with attention on the figure's surroundings (330,140)–(520,230), the lower-left field (180,240)–(460,410), and the corridor approach (300,360)–(520,410). Had to magnify — (300,80)–(560,300) at 3×, (440,14)–(630,200) at 3×, (230,250)–(470,400) at 3×, (360,100)–(440,150) at 6×, (380,280)–(480,345) at 6×. Everything in the second list is invisible in the first.
F1.Q8:
**Laid recently — a year or two — and walked on hard by the crew that laid it.** It reads as exactly one age everywhere; I could not find a region that reads older or younger than any other.

That is the wrong answer for this place by two and a half orders of magnitude.
F1.Q8_WHY:
Age in stone is carried by the transitions, not the faces, and every transition here is new. Slab corners at (445,215), (520,145), (300,255), (405,90) are square to the pixel — no rounding, no chipping, no crushed arrises. Joints across (300,80)–(560,300) are full, even in width, and uninterrupted; nothing has washed out, nothing has been re-packed. No slab is displaced vertically against its neighbour anywhere I looked. There is no dishing along the corridor approach (x378–432, y360–400), where a few centuries of boots would have worn a tray into the stone.

The single-hue finding cuts the same way. Hue standard deviation of 1.23° across the entire floor means no slab has weathered differently from any other, nothing has stained, nothing damp has sat anywhere. Old floors are patchy in colour before they are patchy in shape, and this one is not patchy at all.

The abrasion on the faces is real but it is all shallow and all the same depth, which is what you get from one pass of a texture, not from four hundred years of anything.
F1.Q9:
Route: from the figure at (405,180), straight down the middle through (405,240), (405,300), (400,360), into the corridor mouth at (405,400) and south into the dark.

**The floor told me nothing.** I routed by the walls and by the edge of the torchlight, and only by those.
F1.Q9_WHY:
Along the route — (405,240), (405,300), (400,360), (405,400) — the ground is the same warm sandstone at the same mark density as everything beside it. The regions I rejected — the left field around (230,250), the right field around (570,250), the upper courses around (450,60) — are *also* the same. I compared them cell by cell in the relative-detail map and there is no measurable difference between the ground on my route and the ground I chose not to walk on. The corridor mouth at (378–432, 400–440), which every soul filed through this place would have to cross, has the same hatch density as the far corner at (600,80), which leads nowhere.

Nothing is polished. Nothing is scuffed more. There is no drag scar, no cart rut, no darkened lane. The floor has no memory of anyone.
F1.Q10:
Only one opening is inside the light: the south corridor at x378–432. The rest of the room's boundary is beyond the torch, so I can't judge those.

For the one I can see: the ground in front of it is indistinguishable from the ground everywhere else. Same hue, same value once the falloff is corrected, same mark density in the 16×16 detail map. If this is the way in and out of a room in a place under continuous heavy use, the floor does not admit it.

---
F1.CULL: Every slab is scuffed identically — uniform texture noise, no traffic, no history, no wear anywhere.
F1.FLIP LIST:
- Cut a traffic lane: polish the slabs along the south corridor approach (roughly x370–440, y240–400) smoother and darker than their neighbours, and thin the surface marks to near-zero in that lane so the route is visible before the walls are.
- Replace the drawn arcs — including the one with a flat 28px apex at y301, x425–452 — with real fractures: varying width, a visible origin, branching, spalled ends, and a slab edge displaced across the break.
- Texture the ~8 blank slabs at (530,214), (517,87), (372,125), (477,179), (455,217), (340,304), (200,293), or commit to them as deliberate features — sunken, lifted, or missing, with a visible edge — so they stop being the loudest thing on screen for no reason.
- Break the single-hue lock: shift a minority of slabs off hue 28° toward cooler grey and desaturate them, so the floor stops reading as one uniform new-laid batch and starts reading as stone replaced piecemeal over centuries.
- Move detail from the face to the edges: round and chip the slab corners, wash out and re-pack sections of joint, and drop the per-face hatch density by at least half — the marks are invisible at 1:1 and only make the surface read as woven cloth.

---

F2.Q1: Cut stone slabs — brick-shaped flags, dry-laid in a rough running bond. I can tell it's stone and I can tell it's cut rather than natural. I cannot tell you *which* stone, and that's the problem: it has no grain, no bedding, no colour, no mineral. It is "generic dungeon slab."
F2.Q1_WHY: The joint network at (196–620, 30–390) is continuous, dark, and consistent-width — that's mortarless flagging, not planks or packed earth. Slab pitch is ~37px with slabs subdivided into halves and thirds. But I measured the face colour across 108 tiles after normalising out the lamp falloff: mean normalised brightness 0.997, **std 0.076**; R/B hue ratio 2.073, **std 0.216** — and the hue outliers are near-black tiles where the ratio is noise. Every slab on this floor is the same value and the same colour as every other slab. One material, mixed nowhere, stained nowhere, replaced nowhere.
F2.Q2:
South, into the corridor at (330–430, 395+).

Nothing about the ground influenced that. I picked it because it is the only opening whose far end I cannot see — the west corridor at (0–185, 150–290) is already visible to its edge, so south is the only unexplored direction. That is a wall-and-camera decision, not a floor decision. I want to be plain about this: I looked at the ground in front of both mouths specifically to see if it would break the tie, and it did not.
F2.Q3:
Something has been applied to it. Nothing has happened to it.

It carries three marks: dark round patches ~22–28px across, branching cream lines, and a 45° hatch. All three are spread at even intervals over the entire lit area *and* over the unlit corridors. They do not concentrate anywhere, they do not respect the room's shape, they do not respect the doorways, and they do not accumulate where feet would go. Even distribution is the signature of a texture pass, not of use. This floor has been *aged*; it has not been *used*.
F2.Q3_WHY: I removed the lamp's radial falloff and mapped the residual albedo in 40×40 blocks across (200–620, 30–390). Result: everything sits within ±10 of a ~100 mean, i.e. under 10%, with no coherent structure — no darker lane, no lighter lane, no polished centre, no grime at the edges. And the ~15 dark patches are spaced roughly one per seven slabs with no clustering — including in the south corridor at (330–430, 400–560), which under the fiction is a throat that four hundred years of traffic has poured through, and which is textured identically to the middle of the room.
F2.Q4:
Three things, in this order.

1. **The cream squiggles.** Densest at (280–360, 250–320) and (455–520, 55–125). I counted 4,482 pixels on the lit floor sitting more than 25 levels above their local surround. They do dim with the lamp, but their *contrast ratio against the floor rises with distance* — 1.4× at 20–60px from the light, 2.2× at 220–260px. So in the outer dark, they are the only thing left visible: a field of disconnected glowing worms floating on near-black. My eye went to them before it went to the character.

2. **The two blank slabs.** (373–410, 120–145), directly above the figure — the single most-lit tile on the screen, and it is a flat empty rectangle. And (530–590, 205–235), a double-width slab with literally zero surface detail. In a field where every neighbour is hatched, these read as holes in the art, not as smooth stone.

3. **The dark patches wearing dotted cream necklaces.** At high zoom, e.g. (325–375, 20–70), the bright rim runs *all the way around* the patch as a broken dotted contour. That is an outline, not a rim light. A hole or a scorch lit by a lamp 150px to the lower-right would have a crescent on one side. This has a necklace. Once I saw it on one, I saw it on all fifteen.
F2.Q5:
**Repeated.** Not by literal tile duplication — I checked, and the honest result is in the work's favour: I ran normalised cross-correlation on 3,521 24×24 patches across the whole floor, and the top non-adjacent match was 0.94 at (206,288)/(254,288), which on inspection is two low-contrast dark patches sharing a joint line, not a copied tile. The blobs are individually varied too: template-matching the blob at (392,222) against the entire floor returned a best non-self score of 0.52. No two tiles are the same tile.

It is repeated at the level above that — the vocabulary. I histogrammed gradient orientation over the whole lit floor: energy piles up at 0°/90° (11,609 and 11,631 samples) and at 45°/135° (6,025 and 5,735), with every off-axis bin under 1,000. Roughly 92% of every mark on this surface lies on one of four axes. Each tile then draws from a set of four states — 45° hatch, vertical comb-ticks, 1px random noise, or blank — and the hatch is the same angle and the same ~5px spacing everywhere it appears, from (500–590, 20–130) to (536,217) to (255–360, 70–110). Real tooling marks vary per slab because a different hand cut each slab on a different day. These do not vary. The randomness is in the pixels; the decisions are all the same decision.
F2.Q6:
**YES.** The lighting falloff is clean and correctly warm, the bond pattern varies its slab widths, and nothing is visibly broken.

**Merely competent.** Not good. A good floor gives you information you didn't ask it for. This one gives you none — I ran three separate measurements looking for something the ground was telling me, and each came back flat.
F2.Q7:
**The faces are blank at 1:1.** What I could read without magnifying: the joint grid, the cream squiggles, and the dark patches. That's the whole list, and note that two of those three are *joints and blobs*, not the face of the material.

What I only got by magnifying: the 45° hatch — at 1:1 it does not read as tooling or as anything else, it reads as undifferentiated grubbiness. The vertical comb-ticks, which I did not see at all at 1:1 and which look like inscribed tallies at 6×. The single-pixel noise dither. And the fact that the blob rims are dotted rather than solid.

There is a scale problem underneath this. I sampled the character sprite's pixels at (391–392, 161–162) and (399–400, 161–162): the sprite is drawn in **2×2 pixel blocks**. The floor's noise dither at (430–490, 140–200) is drawn in **1×1 pixels**. The floor's detail is authored at half the character's pixel size, so it physically cannot survive to the same viewing distance. That is why the faces read as mush.
F2.Q7_WHY: Checked at 1:1 — (185–630, 15–395) whole room; specifically (350–500, 120–270) around the figure, (480–630, 40–190), (200–350, 260–410). Had to magnify — (430–490, 140–200) at 10× to find the noise dither; (240–360, 60–180) at 6× to resolve the hatch and the comb-ticks; (325–375, 20–70) at 8× to see the rims were dotted contours; (505–600, 195–240) at 8× to confirm the blank slab was blank rather than dark.
F2.Q8:
It reads as **one age everywhere**, and that age is *unspecified* — I cannot give you a number, because the floor does not contain the evidence a number would come from.

What it does not have: a single replaced slab, a single patch, a single repair. No rope, no driven pin, no salvaged timber, no hide. Nothing settled, nothing tilted, nothing lipped up so you'd trip. No second stone. No edge worn round while its neighbour stayed sharp. Slab-to-slab normalised brightness varies by std 0.076 — under 8% — and hue not at all.

If I have to answer: it reads as **laid all at once and untouched since**, which is exactly the age the fiction says it cannot be. A frontier held for four hundred years by a company that repairs everything with whatever is to hand should leave the ground as the most heavily annotated surface in the game. This ground is the least annotated surface in the frame.
F2.Q8_WHY: (200–615, 32–385), 108 tiles sampled on a 37px grid after lighting normalisation — brightness std 0.076, range 0.753–1.244, and both extremes are the two blank slabs at (373–410, 120–145) and (530–590, 205–235), not stone of a different age. Joint width and slab pitch are constant from (200,35) to (600,380). The mouth of the south corridor at (335–425, 390–410) is cut with the same crisp joints as the room's interior at (400, 200).
F2.Q9:
From the west mouth at ~(185, 220), east across the room's middle band through (250, 215) → (330, 210) → (400, 230), then turn south at ~(390, 300) and down through (390, 350) into the corridor throat at (380, 400).

**The ground told me nothing. I routed by the walls alone.** Every metre of that path is indistinguishable from every metre I rejected.
F2.Q9_WHY: Along the route — (185–430, 200–240) and (365–420, 240–400). Rejected — (200–320, 40–120) upper-left, (480–620, 40–190) upper-right, (200–330, 300–390) lower-left. What is different about the ground between them: nothing I can measure. All six regions carry the same slab pitch, the same joint value, the same hatch angle, the same blob frequency, and the same normalised albedo to within the 7.6% tile-to-tile spread. My residual map covers exactly these regions and the route blocks are not brighter, darker, smoother, or dirtier than the rejected ones. I chose the middle band because it is the shortest line between two doors, which is a statement about the doors.
F2.Q10:
**They all look the same.** I can't rank them.

Judging only the ground in front of each: the west mouth at (150–210, 190–260) and the south mouth at (335–425, 385–420) have identical slab pitch, identical joint treatment, and the same scattered dark patches at the same frequency. The south corridor's interior at (330–430, 430–580) — which I lifted with a gamma pass to see past the darkness — carries the same blobs and the same cracks at the same density as the middle of the room. Nothing is polished, nothing is grooved, no threshold is dished, no mouth is dirtier or cleaner than the other. If one of these is a dead end nobody has opened in a century and the other is the road the garrison walks daily, the floor does not know it.
F2.CULL: Reject — the ground records no traffic, no repair, and no age; three exits read identically.
F2.FLIP LIST:
- Wear the traffic in: darken and smooth the slab faces along the west-mouth→south-mouth line at (185–430, 200–240) and (365–420, 240–400), and leave the corners at (200–320, 40–120) and (200–330, 300–390) sharp-jointed and rough — a measurable albedo split of at least 20%, not the current 7.6%.
- Put orc repair on the ground: at minimum three patches — a replaced slab in a different stone value, a plank-and-driven-pin bridge over a broken flag, a rope-lashed timber shim — sited near the south mouth at (350–430, 360–400) where the load is.
- Redraw the dark patches: replace the full dotted cream necklace (see (325–375, 20–70)) with a single crescent whose side is driven by the lamp position, and cut their count from ~15 to 5 so they read as specific events rather than as scatter.
- Kill the blank slabs at (373–410, 120–145) and (530–590, 205–235), and either give the 45° hatch a per-slab angle and spacing or remove it — at 1:1 it reads as grubbiness, not as tooling.
- Author the floor at the character's pixel scale: the sprite uses 2×2 pixel blocks, the floor uses 1×1, so no face detail survives to viewing distance. Redraw the surface at 2× and let the cream cracks drop below the joint value so they stop out-reading the character.

Forward look: the fix that changes the most per unit of work is the wear pass — one albedo split along the walked line would answer Q2, Q9 and Q10 at once, and it can go in before any tile is redrawn. The pixel-scale mismatch is the expensive one and it invalidates any face detail authored before it's settled, so I'd resolve that before commissioning new tiles.
